lesson.title: NAT64: Letting IPv6 Only Devices Reach an IPv4 World
lesson.summary: NAT64 lets a device on an IPv6 only network reach servers that are still IPv4 only, translating packets between the two address families at a gateway, which makes it a key tool for networks migrating away from IPv4.
lesson.body:
The internet is in a long, uneven transition from IPv4 to IPv6, and that unevenness creates a real, practical problem. A mobile carrier or a newly built network might choose to run IPv6 only internally, since it is simpler to operate one address family instead of two and IPv6 avoids the address exhaustion that IPv4 suffers from. But a huge share of servers on the internet are still reachable only over IPv4, and an IPv6 only device has no ordinary way to open a connection to an address in a completely different address family. NAT64 is a transition mechanism built specifically to bridge that gap.

The idea builds directly on ordinary NAT's core trick of rewriting addresses at a gateway, except that instead of translating between private and public addresses within the same address family, NAT64 translates between address families entirely, from IPv6 to IPv4 and back. To make this work, a NAT64 gateway represents the whole IPv4 address space as a range of addresses inside an IPv6 prefix, most commonly the well known prefix 64:ff9b::/96, defined specifically for this purpose. An IPv4 address can be embedded directly into the low order bits of an IPv6 address built on that prefix, which gives every IPv4 destination a corresponding, synthetic IPv6 address that IPv6 only devices can actually address packets to.

NAT64 is normally paired with a companion service called DNS64 to make this transparent to applications. When an IPv6 only client looks up the name of an IPv4 only server and no ordinary IPv6 address, an AAAA record, exists for it, DNS64 finds the server's IPv4 address instead and synthesizes an AAAA record that embeds it inside the 64:ff9b::/96 prefix, handing that back to the client as if it were a normal IPv6 address. The client, with no idea any translation is happening, sends its packets to that synthetic IPv6 address. Those packets reach the NAT64 gateway, which strips the IPv6 header, extracts the embedded IPv4 address, builds an IPv4 packet addressed to the real server, and rewrites the source address to one of its own public IPv4 addresses, tracking the connection in a translation table exactly the way ordinary NAT and port address translation do. The IPv4 server's reply comes back to the gateway, which reverses the process and delivers a properly formed IPv6 packet to the original client.

NAT64 matters as a transition tool precisely because it lets a network commit to IPv6 internally without cutting itself off from the still largely IPv4 rest of the internet, buying time for IPv4 only servers to add IPv6 support at their own pace while IPv6 only clients keep working today.
